titleText.noteEn: The official English title text drops the h sounds in 'ardly and 'er, making the end of supercollider sound like “collide 'er” and invoking the stock “I hardly know her” joke; its two spaces after the question mark are preserved exactly. The Spanish archive keeps the flirtatious formula with la even though supercolisionador is grammatically masculine, so it is a deliberately nonliteral and grammatically playful adaptation rather than a direct Spanish pun.

cardDefinitions.noteEn: Enciende is the present form of encender for one person or thing. With se, encenderse describes a device or system starting up without naming whoever activates it.

Podría is a form of poder used for an imagined possibility. To make this form, poder changes to podr- and adds -ía. The same written form can mean “I could” or can go with one other person or thing; the stated subject shows which meaning applies.

Fastidies is the special form of fastidiar used after no to tell one familiar person not to bother or annoy someone. The complete exclamation no fastidies also has a common idiomatic use taught separately.
Empezado is the completed-action form of empezar, “to start.” It follows a form of haber in expressions such as han empezado, “they have started.”

cardDefinitions.answerEn: they will do; they will make
cardDefinitions.noteEn: Harán is the future form of hacer used with ellos or ellas. The same form can also mean “you all will do” with ustedes when the listeners are the subject.

example.en: They will do the work tomorrow.

cardDefinitions.noteEn: Dicho is the irregular completed-action form of decir, “to say.” After a form of haber, it corresponds to English “said.”
Estudiante can refer to a male or female student; the surrounding article or other context can show gender when it matters.

cardDefinitions.answerEn: no separate English word; links ir to marcha in ir de marcha
cardDefinitions.noteEn: The de is required in the fixed expression ir de marcha, which means to go out partying. Translating de by itself would hide how the expression works.

example.en: We are going out partying on Friday.

cardDefinitions.noteEn: In the fixed expression ir de marcha, marcha refers to lively nightlife or partying rather than a literal march or movement.

example.en: They went out partying last night.

cardDefinitions.answerEn: are you joining; are you up for it (with te and a)
cardDefinitions.noteEn: Apuntas is the present tú form of apuntar. In te apuntas a, the full verb apuntarse means to sign up, join in, or be willing to take part.

cardDefinitions.answerEn: to; for (required after apuntarse before the activity)
cardDefinitions.noteEn: Apuntarse uses a before the plan, event, or activity someone joins or is willing to do.

example.en: I am in for the dinner.

cardDefinitions.answerEn: no separate English word; begins a fondo, “thoroughly” or “all-out”
cardDefinitions.noteEn: The a combines with fondo to form the fixed expression a fondo. Learn the two words together rather than translating this a on its own.
Fondo can mean a bottom or depth. In the fixed expression a fondo, that image becomes the idea of doing something thoroughly, fully, or all-out.
With an article and no following noun, extraño can itself name a male stranger. This differs from the adjective extraño meaning “strange” or “weird.”

example.es: Un extraño llamó a la puerta.
example.en: A stranger knocked at the door.

cardDefinitions.noteEn: Encantador describes a masculine singular person or thing. The feminine singular form is encantadora.
Encima places something in the upper position. It can stand alone when the reference point is understood; encima de names that reference point explicitly.
Invitado is the completed-action form of invitar, “to invite.” With a person and a before a drink or meal, invitar can also mean to treat that person or buy it for them.

example.es: Te he invitado a un café.
example.en: I have treated you to a coffee.

cardDefinitions.answerEn: to; for (introducing what someone is invited to)
cardDefinitions.noteEn: After invitar and the invited person, a introduces the event, activity, food, or drink being offered.
Copa can name a stemmed glass or the alcoholic drink served in one. Invitar a una copa commonly means to buy someone a drink.

example.es: Tomaron una copa después del trabajo.
example.en: They had a drink after work.

cardDefinitions.noteEn: Camarero can refer to a man serving customers in a restaurant or bar. Camarera is the feminine form.
A margarita is a cocktail commonly made with tequila, citrus juice, and orange liqueur. The same Spanish word also means “daisies,” but the bar context selects the drink meaning.

example.es: Pidieron dos margaritas en el bar.
example.en: They ordered two margaritas at the bar.

cardDefinitions.questionEn: How do you say “come on!” or “give me a break!” informally when something sounds unbelievable or annoying?
cardDefinitions.answerEn: Use ¡No fastidies! as an informal exclamation of disbelief, protest, or annoyance.
cardDefinitions.noteEn: The words literally form a negative command from fastidiar, “to bother or annoy.” As a fixed reaction, however, the expression often challenges what was just said rather than asking someone to stop a specific act. It is informal and can sound sharper than a neutral response.

example.es: ¡No fastidies! Eso no puede ser verdad.
example.en: Come on! That cannot be true.

cardDefinitions.questionEn: How do you refer to a completed action when the surrounding sentence treats it as uncertain, denied, desired, or otherwise not simply stated as fact?
cardDefinitions.answerEn: Use the matching special form of haber—haya, hayas, hayamos, hayáis, or hayan—then the action verb's completed-action form.
cardDefinitions.noteEn: These special haber forms belong to what is called the subjunctive, used when a clause is framed through uncertainty, denial, wishes, or similar attitudes rather than asserted directly. The completed-action form, called the past participle, stays unchanged: haya hablado, hayas comido, hayan vivido. Only haber changes for the person or group.

example.es: No conozco a nadie que haya visitado Perú.
example.en: I do not know anyone who has visited Peru.

cardDefinitions.questionEn: How do you say that someone goes out partying?
cardDefinitions.answerEn: Use a matching form of ir, then de marcha.
cardDefinitions.noteEn: Ir changes for the person and time: voy, vas, vamos, fueron, and so on. De marcha stays together and refers to going out for lively nightlife or partying, not to marching somewhere.

example.en: We are going out partying on Saturday.

cardDefinitions.questionEn: How do you say that someone signs up for, joins, or is willing to take part in a plan?
cardDefinitions.answerEn: Use the matching small pronoun and form of apuntarse, then a and the plan or activity.
cardDefinitions.noteEn: The small pronoun changes with the person: me apunto, te apuntas, se apunta, nos apuntamos. The a introduces what that person joins. The plus sign in the prompt means “followed by,” and the rest of the prompt names the plan or activity that fills that slot.

cardDefinitions.questionEn: How do you say that something is done thoroughly, fully, or all-out?
cardDefinitions.answerEn: Use a fondo to describe going to the fullest extent or depth.
cardDefinitions.noteEn: Fondo literally suggests a bottom or depth. In this fixed expression, that image conveys thoroughness or full intensity. The exact English wording changes with what is being described: study a subject thoroughly, clean deeply, or go all-out.

cardDefinitions.questionEn: How do you say that someone invites a person to an event or treats them to food or a drink?
cardDefinitions.answerEn: Use invitar for the invitation, identify the invited person, then use a before the event, activity, food, or drink.
cardDefinitions.noteEn: Alguien means the person invited and algo means what they are invited to; they are placeholders, not words that must appear literally. A name often has a before it: invito a Marta. An object pronoun can replace the person: te invito. The second a introduces the invitation or treat.

example.en: I will treat you to a coffee.

cardDefinitions.questionEn: How do you say that a container or place is full all the way to the top?
cardDefinitions.answerEn: Use hasta arriba to mean filled to the top or completely full.
cardDefinitions.noteEn: Hasta gives the endpoint and arriba supplies the upper limit. With a container it can be literal; with a place such as a bus or bar, it can also mean packed or completely full.

example.es: La caja está llena hasta arriba.
example.en: The box is full to the top.

cardDefinitions.answerEn: Natural cosmic rays already produce very energetic particle collisions, a comparison used to argue that starting the Large Hadron Collider would not create a new planet-destroying danger.
cardDefinitions.noteEn: The opening fear imagines the collider's startup ending life on Earth. The reply invokes cosmic rays, which have struck Earth naturally for an extremely long time, and the physics student treats the alleged catastrophe mostly as an excuse for a party. That contrast supplies the scientific setup for the joke.

cardDefinitions.promptEs: encima o abajo · una copa · hasta arriba
cardDefinitions.answerEn: The flirtation turns a question about being on top or below into sexual-position innuendo, then echoes the vertical wording in an order for drinks filled to the top.
cardDefinitions.noteEn: The joke escalates unusually quickly from an invitation to a positional question. The response retreats to the convention of first buying someone a drink, but the final order keeps the above-and-below vocabulary active. The Spanish adaptation uses margaritas and hasta arriba, so its closing wordplay differs from the official English whiskey-sour wording.

excludedUnits.rationale: LHC is the international English-derived acronym for the Large Hadron Collider, not a Spanish lexical word occurrence.

applications.explanationEn: Oye is the familiar singular command form of oír, used here to get the listener's attention.
Esta names one situation as the subject, so podría expresses what that situation could or might be rather than what the speaker could do.
Podría carries the imagined possibility, while ser remains in its unchanged dictionary form.

applications.explanationEn: No comes before fastidies, the special negative-command form used to address one familiar listener.
The two-word exclamation reacts with dismissive disbelief rather than making a literal request about one specific annoyance.
Ni and siquiera combine to rule out even the minimal stage being discussed.
Han is the helper form for the implied plural subject, and empezado is the unchanged completed-action form.
Hacer uses its irregular future stem har- plus the plural ending -án.

applications.exampleEs: NO HARÁN NADA QUE NO HAYAN
applications.explanationEn: No harán nada denies that any qualifying action exists, so que is followed by the special form hayan. The second no belongs inside the description but is not what creates the negated antecedent.
Hayan is the plural special form of haber required by the denied description, and hecho is hacer's unchanged completed-action form.

applications.explanationEn: Para introduces the purpose, and ir stays in its unchanged dictionary form.
Ir is the unchanged form required after para, while de marcha supplies the fixed partying meaning.

Hasta sets an endpoint and arriba makes that endpoint the top, expressing complete fullness.
